messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 21
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Unemployed
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 42

**Case Vignette: “Marcus”**

Marcus is a 21-year-old married European male who presents as quiet and watchful, his eyes often scanning the room as if tracking an invisible threat. He is currently unemployed, having dropped out of a welding apprenticeship three months ago. He lives with his wife, Elena, in a small apartment. He describes his life as having “stopped” on a specific Tuesday afternoon last spring.

The trauma did not happen to Marcus. It happened to his younger brother, Leo, who was 17 at the time. Marcus was driving them home from a job site where Leo had been helping him. A semi-truck ran a red light and T-boned the passenger side of Marcus’s pickup. The crash was violent—glass, metal, the sound of tearing steel. Marcus remembers the impact, the smell of gasoline, and then the silence. He turned to see Leo unconscious, his face bloodied, his body crumpled against the shattered door.

Marcus remembers screaming his brother’s name. He remembers crawling out of his own window, his leg bleeding, and trying to pull Leo from the wreckage. He remembers the paramedics prying him away. Leo survived, but with a traumatic brain injury and a fractured spine. He spent six weeks in the ICU and is now in a rehabilitation facility, learning to walk and speak again.

In the weeks immediately following the accident, Marcus was the picture of strength. He stayed at the hospital every night. He spoke to doctors, made phone calls, and held his mother while she cried. He told himself he had to be the rock. But about a month in, something shifted. He began to feel as though he were watching himself from a great distance. The world felt muffled, like sounds were coming through water. He stopped being able to sleep. He started having the dream—the exact moment of impact, over and over, but in the dream, he is always too slow. He sees Leo’s face shatter, and he wakes up gasping, drenched in sweat.

Now, Marcus cannot drive. The mere sight of his truck keys on the counter makes his heart pound so hard he feels dizzy. He avoids the intersection where the accident happened, taking three-bus detours that add an hour to any errand. He has not visited his brother in two weeks. He tells himself it is because he is “too busy,” but the truth is that the smell of the rehabilitation center—antiseptic and stale coffee—triggers a wave of nausea and a feeling of unreality. He feels a deep, corrosive guilt. He was the driver. He was supposed to protect Leo. He replays the moment constantly: *If I had left five seconds later. If I had looked left again.*

Elena, his wife of only eight months, is struggling. She tells him he is “not here anymore,” and he knows she is right. He has become irritable, snapping at her for small things—the volume of the television, the way she chews. He feels a constant, low-grade anger that has no target. He has withdrawn from his small circle of friends. He stopped answering texts. He quit the apprenticeship because he could not concentrate on the blueprints; the welding torch’s hiss sounded too much like the air escaping the truck’s tires.

Today, he sits in the therapy room with his hands clasped tightly in his lap. He says he feels “hollowed out.” He is not suicidal, he insists, but he has a pervasive sense that his life is already over, that the best version of himself died in that truck. He has lost fifteen pounds. He has not had a full night of sleep in two months. He is terrified of the future, not because of his own unemployment, but because he cannot stop imagining Leo’s future—a future of wheelchairs and speech therapy. He carries the weight of his brother’s suffering as if it were his own, and he does not know how to put it down.
